title: Bad trees cannot bear good fruit
source_text: THESIS I. CHRISTUS non uno in loco pronunciat malam arborem non posse facere bonos fructus. Porro homines universi per naturam arbores malae sunt. Quippe in peccato nati sunt & concepti, & sensus ac cogitatio cordis humani ad malum prona est a pueritia, ut Deus ipse apud Mosem testatur cap. 6. Gen. Ac proinde ab hominibus, si sibi ipsis relinquantur, nullum opus procedere potest vere bonum & Deo gratum, & quod sit ad salutem alicujus momenti: sed quicquid homines absque Dei gratia, & solius naturae viribus cogitant, aut faciunt, quantumcunque exterius splendere videatur, semper tamen intus aliquid putre habet, unde simpliciter vitiosum redditur.
pass_a_gloss: THESIS I. CHRIST in more than one place declares that a bad tree cannot bear good fruits. Now all men by nature are bad trees. For they are born & conceived in sin, & the sense & thought of the human heart is prone to evil from childhood, as God himself testifies in Moses chap. 6. Gen. And therefore from men, if they are left to themselves, no work can proceed that is truly good & pleasing to God, & that is of any moment for salvation: but whatever men think, or do without the grace of God, & by the powers of nature alone, however much it may seem to shine outwardly, yet always has something rotten within, whence it is rendered simply vicious.
pass_b_english: Thesis I. Christ says more than once that a bad tree cannot produce good fruit. By nature every human being is a bad tree: we are conceived and born in sin, and, as God himself testifies through Moses in Genesis 6, the human heart's every feeling and thought leans toward evil from childhood.

So if people are left to themselves, no work can come from them that is truly good, pleasing to God, and of any value for salvation. Whatever they think or do without God's grace, by natural strength alone, may look splendid from outside, but there is always something rotten inside it, and that makes it simply faulty.

choices.why: Christ's image of the good and the bad tree (Matt. 7:17-18), which frames the whole locus: the person must be made good before the works can be.
